Neyveli: The Town That Raised Me and Then Forgot Itself

# Neyveli: The Town That Raised Me and Then Forgot Itself

### By a former resident of Block-2, Jawahar School survivor, Central Library addict, and lifelong beneficiary of a town built by people who believed planning was a virtue.

There are places we leave behind.

And then there are places that never quite leave us.

Neyveli belongs firmly to the second category.

I have lived in larger cities. I have worked in places with glass towers, climate-controlled offices, imported coffee machines, and management consultants who charge by the minute to explain concepts that Neyveli understood sixty years ago.

Yet every time I return to Neyveli, I am struck by the same thought:

*“How did a lignite mine produce a better civilization than most modern cities?”*

That question has haunted me for years.

Because Neyveli was never supposed to exist.

It certainly wasn’t supposed to be beautiful.

The raw material beneath its soil was lignite—a fuel so unfashionable that even coal looks down upon it. It is the brown bread of fossil fuels. The government dug it out of the ground, burnt it in enormous boilers, and generated electricity for millions.

Yet somehow, in the process of building a mine, they accidentally built a town.

And not just any town.

They built one of the finest townships India has ever seen.

The tragedy is that we are now quietly dismantling it.

## A Childhood Without Traffic

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The first thing outsiders notice about Neyveli is the silence.

The second thing they notice is the trees.

The third thing they notice is that the silence is caused by the trees.

Modern Indian cities operate on a simple urban-planning principle:

Cut the trees first. Regret it later.

Neyveli followed a different philosophy.

The planners planted trees as though they were being paid by the leaf.

Tamarind trees.

Neem trees.

Copperpods.

Rain trees.

Gulmohars.

Entire armies of trees.

By the time I was growing up, these trees had matured into giant green cathedrals arching over the roads.

In summer, when the rest of Tamil Nadu resembled a giant dosa tawa, Neyveli remained improbably cool.

Visitors from Chennai would step out of the bus and ask suspiciously:

“Is it raining somewhere nearby?”

No.

That was just what happened when urban planners possessed common sense.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Greatest Luxury We Never Knew We Had

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Children are notoriously bad at appreciating privilege.

I certainly was.

Growing up, I assumed everyone had enormous playgrounds.

I assumed everyone had libraries.

I assumed everyone could cycle safely from one end of town to another.

I assumed everyone had uninterrupted electricity.

I assumed everyone had parks.

I assumed everyone had functioning drainage.

I assumed everyone had trees.

Then I left Neyveli.

And I discovered that most of India was conducting an entirely different experiment.

In many cities, crossing the road requires courage normally associated with military operations.

In others, parks exist only in municipal brochures.

Libraries are viewed as heritage structures because nobody has entered them voluntarily since 1987.

Footpaths are either occupied, excavated, or mythical.

Neyveli, meanwhile, had solved these problems before I was born.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The University of Rain Trees

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

My real education did not occur inside classrooms.

Please do not tell my teachers.

It happened beneath rain trees.

It happened in libraries.

It happened on bicycles.

The Central Library was perhaps the most important institution in my life after my family.

During scorching summer afternoons, when the sensible part of Tamil Nadu slept, many of us disappeared into that building.

The library was air-conditioned by a technology now largely forgotten:

Trees.

Lots of them.

Combined with thick walls and common sense.

I spent countless afternoons wandering among shelves that smelled faintly of paper, dust, glue, and possibility.

The librarians knew us.

The books knew us.

Sometimes I suspect the books raised us.

Long before social media began manufacturing opinions at industrial scale, we developed them the old-fashioned way—by reading.

Under the giant rain trees outside, debates would erupt.

One boy would argue for science.

Another for literature.

Someone would passionately defend cricket statistics.

Someone else would claim Rajinikanth could solve all known policy problems.

The discussions were spirited.

The friendships were genuine.

And nobody asked about caste before lending a book.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Jawahar School: The Factory That Produced Human Beings

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If Neyveli had a soul, it was probably hidden somewhere inside the corridors of Jawahar Higher Secondary School.

Like many alumni, I carry conflicting memories.

Fondness.

Terror.

Affection.

Homework.

Particularly homework.

Jawahar School produced thousands of engineers, doctors, scientists, bankers, professors, researchers, bureaucrats, and occasionally politicians.

No one planned this.

Or perhaps everyone did.

The miracle was not academic excellence.

The miracle was social mixing.

The son of a mine worker sat next to the son of a chief engineer.

The daughter of a clerk competed against the daughter of a senior executive.

Inside the classroom, the hierarchy of the corporation largely disappeared.

Marks were the great socialist equalizer.

Physics showed no respect for designation.

Mathematics did not care about pay scales.

Chemistry ignored housing categories.

And examination papers displayed a refreshing indifference to parental status.

Many of my classmates now live across the world.

America.

Singapore.

Australia.

Europe.

Bengaluru.

Some became distinguished academics.

Others became entrepreneurs.

Many became successful professionals.

Yet when Neyveli alumni meet, conversations quickly regress to the intellectual maturity level of Class IX.

This is one of the township’s greatest achievements.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Secularism of Everyday Life

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Politicians frequently lecture us about secularism.

Neyveli quietly practiced it.

Nobody issued press releases.

Nobody organized conferences.

Nobody conducted television debates.

People simply lived together.

Children celebrated every festival because festivals usually involved sweets.

Religious identities existed.

But they did not dominate.

A Brahmin boy borrowed notes from a Christian girl.

A Muslim student captained the cricket team.

A Dalit engineer supervised projects alongside everyone else - the term dalit was not known then.

The township had bigger priorities.

Examinations.

Promotions.

Water supply.

Cricket.

Electricity.

And whether the canteen’s masala vadai had improved.

The secularism of Neyveli was not ideological.

It was practical.

The mines had no interest in your caste.

The turbines did not care about your religion.

The lignite burned with admirable impartiality.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Tuesdays Were Sacred

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Officially, India has many festivals.

Unofficially, Neyveli had another.

Pay-Day Tuesday.

Anyone who grew up there remembers it.

The market transformed into a carnival.

Farmers arrived from surrounding villages.

Vendors appeared from nowhere.

Families emerged from every block.

The smell of roasted cashews drifted through the air.

Fresh vegetables competed with filter coffee.

Children negotiated desperately for toys.

Parents negotiated desperately against buying them.

The market wasn’t merely commercial.

It was social.

It reminded everyone that Neyveli, despite its modernity, remained connected to the villages around it.

The township and its surroundings breathed together.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When Success Became the Problem

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The irony of Neyveli is that it succeeded too well.

The schools worked.

The libraries worked.

The hospitals worked.

The infrastructure worked.

The result?

Its children left.

Not because they hated Neyveli.

Because Neyveli prepared them to leave.

My generation discovered engineering colleges.

Then IT companies.

Then global careers.

Soon the brightest students were boarding trains to Chennai, Bengaluru, Mumbai, and beyond.

Parents celebrated.

They should have.

This was the entire purpose of education.

Yet each success story removed another family from the township.

The town that raised achievers slowly began exporting them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Empty Quarter Problem

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Nothing prepares you for the sadness of seeing empty quarters.

As a child, every house seemed alive.

Every veranda contained conversations.

Every street contained bicycles.

Every playground contained arguments.

Today many houses stand locked.

Silent.

Patient.

Waiting.

The absurdity is difficult to ignore.

India faces housing shortages.

Cities struggle with affordability.

Young professionals pay astronomical rents.

Contract workers live in crowded settlements outside township limits.

Inside Neyveli, thousands of solid houses sit empty.

If Franz Kafka had worked in a public-sector undertaking, he might have written this policy.

The bureaucracy has achieved a remarkable feat:

It has simultaneously produced homelessness and emptiness.

This requires talent.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Smart Cities and Other Jokes

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One of the great entertainments of modern India is listening to urban planners discuss “smart cities.”

They speak reverently about concepts like:

Walkability.

Green cover.

Mixed-use development.

Traffic calming.

Water recycling.

Neighborhood planning.

Community spaces.

Every time I hear this, I want to hand them a bicycle and say:

“Please spend one afternoon in Neyveli.”

The town implemented these ideas when computers occupied entire rooms and mobile phones belonged to science fiction.

What consultants now present in PowerPoint slides existed naturally in Block 5, Block 10, Block 17, and every other block.

Neyveli was a smart city before smart cities became a government scheme.

The difference is that nobody called it one.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Library Still Waits

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

When I visit today, I often find myself drawn back to the Central Library.

The building remains.

The shelves remain.

The memories certainly remain.

I can almost see the younger version of myself wandering through the aisles.

A boy with more curiosity than direction.

A boy discovering history, literature, politics, science, and satire.

A boy who had no idea how fortunate he was.

The chairs are quieter now.

The discussions beneath the rain trees have thinned.

But the building still waits.

Patiently.

Like the town itself.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What Neyveli Really Produced

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

People often say Neyveli produced electricity.

That is technically true.

It produced millions of megawatts.

It powered industries.

It powered homes.

It powered economic growth.

But electricity was merely the by-product.

Neyveli’s real output was human beings.

Confident human beings.

Educated human beings.

Curious human beings.

People who believed public institutions could work.

People who grew up in a town where libraries mattered.

Where schools mattered.

Where parks mattered.

Where trees mattered.

Where civic life mattered.

That may be the rarest product of all.

## The Town That Still Waits

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Every evening, somewhere in Neyveli, the tamarind trees still sway in the breeze.

The roads remain improbably wide.

The parks remain improbably green.

The library remains improbably hopeful.

The township is older now.

Perhaps a little lonelier.

But not defeated.

When I walk through those familiar streets, I do not see a failed experiment.

I see a forgotten success.

A town built by a generation that believed government could create beauty.

A town that nurtured thousands of lives, including mine.

A town that deserves better than demolition tenders and bureaucratic indifference.

Neyveli’s greatest resource was never the lignite buried beneath it.

It was the civilization built above it.

And if India is wise, it will preserve that civilization before the last rain tree, the last library reader, and the last old resident become footnotes in a report.

Because towns like Neyveli are not built often.

And once lost, they are almost impossible to rebuild.
